method.method_draft: Use central angles and chord-length formulas. From the text, the minor arc length $BC$ is $r$ on a circle of radius $r$, so its central angle is $r/r=1$ radian. Since $AB=AC$, point $A$ must lie on one of the two arc midpoints determined by $B$ and $C$. The condition $AB>r$ rules out the midpoint of the minor arc, because that would give a short chord; therefore $A$ is the midpoint of the major arc. Thus the central angle subtending chord $AB$ is $\pi-\frac12$. Compute $BC=2r\sin(1/2)$ and $AB=2r\sin((\pi-1/2)/2)=2r\cos(1/4)$. Then simplify $AB/BC=\cos(1/4)/\sin(1/2)=1/(2\sin(1/4))=\frac12\csc(1/4)$.

method.method_draft: Use the inscribed angle theorem and the geometry of an isosceles triangle. The minor arc $BC$ has length $r$ on a radius-$r$ circle, so the central angle over minor arc $BC$ is $1$ radian. Because $AB=AC$ and $AB>r$, $A$ is the point on the circle opposite the minor arc $BC$, so the inscribed angle $\angle BAC$ intercepts the minor arc $BC$. Hence $\angle BAC=\frac12$ radian. In isosceles triangle $ABC$ with equal sides $AB=AC=x$, drop the altitude from $A$ to $BC$; it bisects both $BC$ and $\angle BAC$. Therefore $BC=2x\sin(\angle BAC/2)=2x\sin(1/4)$. Thus $AB/BC=x/[2x\sin(1/4)]=\frac12\csc(1/4)$.
